newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers, bosses open talks to end protests.
newsitem.headline: French truckers, bosses open talks to end protests.

text.p: French truckers' unions and haulage bosses began negotiations on Thursday on the grievances of striking truckers whose four-day protest blocking roads and petrol depots is showing signs of squeezing the economy.
But chances of a swift agreement to lift the barricades appeared slim as union leaders went into the talks overtly pessimistic.

Roger Poletti of the Communist-led General Workers' Confederation (CGT) said he doubted the talks would address the unions' demands for wage hikes, shorter working hours and retirement at 55 instead of 60.
"I fear there won't be anything to negotiate, at least not today," he told reporters as he went in to the meeting.
"What is certain is that if we come out of this meeting empty-handed, there will be more protests," he said adding that the protests could spread to Paris on Friday.
Haulage bosses have agreed only to discuss the possibility of early retirement packages and paying truckers' for time spent loading and unloading, currently not taken into account.
"What they (employers) are ready to discuss does not necessarily correspond to our demands," said Michel Caillaud, head of the National Federation of Truck Drivers (FNCR).
About 50,000 trucks were taking part in Thursday's protests according to the CGT, and the drivers were bent on continuing their action until their demands were met.
"The ball is in their court. We'll continue to barricade the roads until a clear agreement has been negotiated," said Jean-Pierre Prou of the CGT.
Car-maker PSA Peugeot Citroen said it had reduced shifts at several plants because of a shortage of spare parts, and some supermarkets and petrol stations were running low on supplies.

Motorways in and out of 30 towns and cities across the country were blocked by trucks, recalling a 1992 truckers' blockade that paralysed France in a protest against a new points system for driving licences.
But Paris has largely been spared during this year's protests apart from some disruption on Wednesday.

Truckers have singled out Bordeaux, whose mayor is Prime Minister Alain Juppe, as the main focus of protests, causing huge traffic jams on all access roads. Airlines at Bordeaux airport said air freight has been badly hit.
Toulouse, Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Caen, Le Mans and the Franco-German border at Strasbourg were also seriously affected.
Hundreds of police were deployed to keep roads open around the Mediterranean port of Marseille as dozens of trucks headed for the city, France's third largest, police said.
Thousands of other trucks stood idle on parking lots across the country.

In the southeast, truckers prevented access to fuel depots in Porte-les-Valence, Le Pontet and Bassens near Avignon, and a Shell refinery in Berre near Marseille, cutting supplies to service stations in the area.
Depots in the Bordeaux area, the western Calvados department and the port of Rouen were also targeted.

"The effects of the strike are just now beginning to be felt, especially in Bordeaux where several petrol stations have run out of supplies," said Bernard Fragneau, head of security and defence in the southwestern Gironde department.
But he said the strikers had allowed a number of petrol trucks to make deliveries to hospitals, police and emergency workers.
